# Superiority Trials {#sec-superiority-trials}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Define the direction and threshold for superiority.
- Separate statistical and clinical superiority.
:::

## The idea

A superiority design seeks evidence that one intervention performs better than another on a prespecified endpoint. If higher outcome values are favourable and $\Delta=\mu_{new}-\mu_{control}$, a directional hypothesis could compare $\Delta$ with zero or a positive superiority margin. The direction of benefit and alpha convention must be stated.

## When and how to apply it

The minimum difference worth detecting need not equal the statistical null boundary. Planning based on a realistically important effect prevents a large but scientifically uninformative design. Changes to outcome direction require a corresponding change to the signed difference and inequality.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A counselling intervention is expected to reduce HbA1c. With lower values better, define the mean difference sign and the one-sided rejection direction before calculating power.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not treat a statistically positive difference smaller than a prespecified clinically important threshold as automatically clinically meaningful.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Sketch the superiority region for both higher-is-better and lower-is-better outcomes.

## Key message

Superiority requires a prespecified benefit direction and clinically meaningful target effect.
